title: Sunflowers Can't Count, Yet Their Seeds Follow Fibonacci Numbers

parts.text: yet its seeds follow Fibonacci numbers.
each one is the sum of the two before.
Each new seed grows a hundred and thirty-seven and a half degrees
parts.tts: Each new seed grows a hundred and thirty-seven and a half degrees,

parts.text: and the spirals appear on their own.

sources: Spiral counts: a domestic sunflower head with '34 spirals running clockwise and 55 spirals running counterclockwise'; '21 and 34 for a small capitulum, up to 89 and 144 or even 144 and 233 for large ones'. Prusinkiewicz and Lindenmayer, The Algorithmic Beauty of Plants (Springer, 1990), chapter 4, algorithmicbotany.org/papers/abop/abop-ch4.pdf.

How often: in 657 sunflowers, 565 of 768 spiral counts were Fibonacci numbers and nearly 20% did not have Fibonacci structure, hence 'often' rather than 'always'. Swinton, Ochu and the MSI Turing's Sunflower Consortium, Royal Society Open Science 3:160091 (2016).

Rule: Vogel's model places floret n at angle n x 137.5 degrees and radius c x sqrt(n); 'the divergence angle between the position vectors of any two successive florets is constant, 137.5 degrees'. H. Vogel, Mathematical Biosciences 44:179-189 (1979), as given in The Algorithmic Beauty of Plants, eq. 4.1. Golden angle = about 137.508 degrees.

Sensitivity: The Algorithmic Beauty of Plants figure 4.2 compares divergence angles of 137.3, 137.5 ('the correct value') and 137.6 degrees to show 'the critical role of the divergence angle'. The scene draws the same model at 137.3 degrees for the 'nudge' line.
Simplification to note: in the real plant new florets form near the centre and older ones are pushed outward; the scene draws the Vogel model, numbering seeds from the centre out.
